(1) STATIC: tsc 0; npx vitest run 2020/2020 across 132 files (from 2001/130 at boot, +19 tests +2 files); npm run build bundle 645.4 KiB / 750 cap, entry 660,916 B — DOWN 100 B from the S132 baseline 661,016 B, which is proof rather than inference that the wide test-only hash ships zero production bytes. (2) MUTATION: 14/14 CAUGHT, each verified to fire in the INTENDED guard rather than a downstream fixture (checked explicitly for M4, where the first reported error came from sync.test.ts). Matrix covers: dropping a family from the coverage map; adding a new Map family to World; dropping a field from a projection list; adding a field to an already-hashed entity; the wide hash going blind to hp and to chewProgress; removing the id sort; marking a narrow-hashed family 'acknowledged'; restoring each of the three wire strips independently; deleting an entire projection loop; adding hp to Primitive; adding a Record-typed field to World. (3) TWO OF MY OWN GUARDS WERE VACUOUS AND MUTATION FOUND BOTH: M9 (the hp test asserted on a creature that hits trimMirrorCreature's early return, so it could never fail) and the spawnedAtTick characterization (asserted against a fixture value of 0, the exact number the deserializer hardcodes). Both fixed, then re-mutated to CAUGHT. (4) CHECK found my own correction was WRONG in three committed places: 'a Voltkin's expiry is re-derivable from spawnedAtTick, which does ride the wire' is false — spawnedAtTick is not a SerializedCreature field, is never emitted, and rehydrates to 0. I verified that by hand before acting on the reviewer's word. The real consequence is worse: despawnAtTick rehydrates to 0 and a PROMOTED client runs the lifetime gate, so creatureLifecycle deletes every live Voltkin on its first creature tick. NOT fixable by un-stripping (serializeCreature only emits despawnAtTick for chewers), so characterized + logged with the mechanism. (5) MEASURED, not estimated: wire 12,413 B -> 12,821 B = +408 B (+3.3%) on the 12-chewer worst case, 3,563 B under the 16 KiB R1 ceiling, taken by running the guard with the strip both restored and removed. (6) HONEST NEGATIVES: widening found NO latent divergence — both differential harnesses pass even with rngSeed, allocator cursors and primitive colours added; I expected red and did not get it. save.replay.test.ts had asserted not.toContain('chewProgress'), i.e. it had LOCKED IN the bug; inverted rather than deleted so the contract change is visible in the diff. (7) GROK's aliasing finding REFUTED by reading save.ts:646 — serializeCreature returns a fresh literal, so trimMirrorCreature never sees live world objects.

reflexion_entries_to_archive.note: I found a false claim in a docblock, corrected it, and the CORRECTION was false too — 're-derivable from spawnedAtTick, which does ride the wire', about a field that is not on the wire at all. It reached a docblock, a test comment and a commit message before CHECK caught it. The first draft was wrong by guessing; the second was wrong by reading a NEIGHBOURING comment ('re-derivable from spawnedAtTick on the trimmed-rehydrate path') and trusting its premise instead of grepping whether the field was serialized. A correction deserves the same verification as the thing it corrects — more, because it arrives wearing the authority of a fix.

M9 said VACUOUS: restoring the hp strip did not fail the hp test. Not because the assertion was wrong, but because the fixture creature hit trimMirrorCreature's EARLY RETURN and was never destructured. The test exercised a path where the code under test does not run. Every previous vacuity lesson in this repo was about the ASSERTION; this one was about the FIXTURE reaching the branch. Ask which branch the fixture takes, not just what the assertion says.

I derived a coverage contract from 'collection-shaped' fields (Map|Set|Array) and called it derived-from-the-type. Record, ReadonlyMap, WeakMap and Float64Array all walked straight through, and every scalar was outside the contract by construction — including rngSeed, the canonical desync root. Keying on `keyof World` instead is more verbose and completely closed. When a guard enumerates what it RECOGNISES, the escape hatch is everything it does not; enumerate the whole domain and classify.

FAMILY_COVERAGE said hunters: 'hashed'. RALPH deleted the entire hunters projection loop and tsc stayed 0 with every test green, because nothing connected the string to the code. A type-level claim about runtime behaviour needs a runtime witness — exporting the parts list and asserting each 'hashed' family contributes one is what made the label true.

save.replay.test.ts asserted not.toContain('chewProgress'). It was not merely stale: it was a guard whose whole function was to keep a bug in place, and it had been green for 30+ sessions. A passing test is evidence that behaviour is INTENTIONAL, not that it is CORRECT. Inverted rather than deleted, so the contract change shows up in the diff where a reviewer will see it.

The PDR predicted the widened hash would expose latent entity divergence and pre-committed to reporting red-as-found. It went green — twice, including after adding rngSeed and the allocator cursors. Worth recording as a measurement rather than quietly dropping: the sims genuinely agree across entity families, so the value delivered was the TRIPWIRE for future state, not a bug found today.

Seven sessions running. This time it cut both ways: RALPH's F1 was RIGHT and I had to verify it before believing my own committed text was wrong; GROK's aliasing finding was WRONG and I had to read save.ts:646 to refute it rather than accept a plausible-sounding break. Same discipline, opposite outcomes — which is exactly why the rule is about mechanism and not about who is usually right.

Two of P2's four items were wrong AS LOGGED. P2-18 'godly' had been adjudicated a false positive in S30/S33, and re-entered four consecutive handoffs as outstanding work — doing it would have shipped a back-compat regression while looking like housekeeping. The V6-RISK item was cited at the wrong lines and understated a never-built enforcement carrier. A carry-forward is a CLAIM, and it inherits authority from repetition rather than from evidence. Re-verify the item before executing it, especially the small ones — nobody re-derives a one-liner.

The whole 'godly' item rested on 'no live emitter post-S27'. True, and irrelevant: the member is a literal in a WIRE-SERIALIZED union, so the read side must still accept it. Deadness is a property of the emit side; compatibility is a property of the read side. For any union that crosses a wire or a save, 'nothing produces this' never implies 'nothing must consume this'.

The logged item was one stale version literal (v9 vs 15). Fixing it put `--list` output on screen, which revealed a SIBLING test overriding to v10 to exercise a 'newer peer' branch against a v15 host — older, not newer, so it had quietly stopped testing the thing its own title names. Nothing failed, because both live in a non-gating quarantine lane. Version literals in an un-type-checked, non-gating lane rot invisibly and in PAIRS; when you find one, grep the file for the rest and write the invariant down.

MCV hard-failed at session close: I had written verification[] entries of type "file_absent_string", which does not exist. The supported set is file_exists / file_absent / file_contains / file_lacks / grep_count / json_field / syntax_ok / nonce_match — and it is listed in the verifier docstring EIGHT LINES IN, a file I never opened. I pattern-matched off the file_contains entries I had just written and generated a plausible sibling name. Two compounding lessons: (1) an INVENTED IDENTIFIER in a declarative config fails silently at author time — there is no compiler for a JSON string, so the only feedback is the consumer, and I shipped it into two completed priorities before the hook spoke; read the consumer schema before emitting values for it. (2) The near-miss: file_lacks PASSES VACUOUSLY when the file is absent, so an absence-only binding would have gone green on a deleted file. I paired each with a positive file_contains companion. This session mutation-tested every code guard and then hand-wrote un-mutated ASSERTIONS ABOUT those guards — the meta-level guard got none of the scrutiny the object level got.

Six sessions of 'the push is the only way to learn whether CI works' — and when it finally happened, the push landed, GitHub logged the PushEvent, and NO run was created. Every precondition I could probe was satisfied (Actions enabled, workflows active, 32 filtered files matched, public repo, valid YAML, well under the commit threshold, no late arrival). The lesson is not about GitHub: it is that 'the mechanism fired' and 'the outcome happened' are separate propositions, and the project's charter had collapsed them into one sentence. I could not root-cause it and deliberately did not invent a cause — I shipped a verifier instead, because a check that catches the failure is worth more than a theory about it.

`rm -rf dist` was blocked by the guardrail. I did not bypass it — an autonomous-run approval is not approval of a specific destructive command. Forced to solve it without deleting, I found the right answer: read dist/index.html for the entry rather than globbing dist/assets, which is both immune to the orphaned chunks that caused the problem AND already the repo's idiom in check-bundle-size.mjs. The guardrail did not cost me a workaround; it cost me a worse design.

verify-deploy's LIVE carrier failed immediately — not a false alarm: dist/ held two orphaned entry chunks from an interrupted build, so there was genuinely no unambiguous 'local build' to compare against. Refusing to guess between two candidates was the correct behaviour and I kept that strictness. A new check earning its keep before it is even committed is the cheapest possible evidence that it is not decorative.
